messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Ravi, a 58-year-old South Asian male and product manager, has sought help due to persistent symptoms that have been escalating over the past few months. His journey to therapy is deeply rooted in his traumatic experience of torture during a business trip abroad, an event that left lasting scars on both his psyche and daily functioning. Ravi’s trauma began when he was captured by individuals who accused him of espionage, believing he was working for a competing company. During the ordeal, he endured multiple days of intense interrogation and physical abuse. The captors would speak in incomprehensible languages, making Ravi feel isolated and helpless. One particularly vivid memory is of being dragged through dimly lit corridors where sirens blared intermittently, heightening his sense of fear and confusion. These experiences left Ravi with a heightened sensitivity to auditory stimuli, especially the sound of incomprehensible chatter and sirens, as well as the physical sensation of dizziness. Since his return, these triggers have become intrusive parts of his daily life. At work, the constant hum of conversation in the office often feels like an echo of the torture room, causing Ravi to withdraw into himself. He avoids social gatherings and even small talk with colleagues, fearing that any sudden noise might trigger a relapse of those harrowing memories. The sound of sirens from emergency vehicles passing by his window sends waves of anxiety through him, making it difficult for him to focus on work. Ravi’s avoidance behaviors have extended beyond just auditory triggers. He is also acutely aware of the potential threats posed by uniformed individuals or anyone carrying weapons. This has led him to avoid public places where he might encounter law enforcement or military personnel. On one occasion, he left a conference early because he saw a security guard with a badge and gun, which triggered an intense panic attack. To cope with his heightened sense of danger, Ravi constantly monitors his body for any signs of distress. He is always on edge, checking to see if he feels dizzy or lightheaded, convinced that these symptoms are precursors to another traumatic event. Even in the safety of his home, he wakes multiple times during the night to check whether everything is secure. Ravi’s mistrust has deepened since the torture incident. He believes people cannot be trusted and often questions their motives, even those closest to him. His wife has noticed a significant change in his behavior; he becomes visibly anxious when she plans social outings or visits from friends. This has strained their relationship, as Ravi is increasingly isolated and withdrawn. Ravi also harbors deep feelings of intrinsic fault, believing there must be something inherently wrong with him that led to the torture. He carries an overwhelming sense of guilt and inadequacy, convinced that he brought this upon himself. Consequently, he has a pervasive belief that nothing good can happen to him anymore, making it difficult for him to find hope or joy in his daily life. The culmination of these symptoms finally prompted Ravi to seek help when his work performance began to suffer significantly. He found it increasingly challenging to complete tasks and meet deadlines due to his constant state of hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors. His inability to relax, even in familiar surroundings, has made him feel like he is constantly walking on eggshells. Ravi’s journey to therapy represents a fragile hope amidst his pervasive mistrust and negative appraisals. He hopes that with the right support, he can regain some sense of control over his life and find ways to manage his symptoms without feeling as though he is perpetually under threat.
